answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 65 BC – 8 BC · Roman lyric poet of the Augustan age
answer.sourceLine: Horace wrote this in his ‘Epistles’ (Book 1, Epistle 2, to Lollius, line 40, c. 20 BC): the Latin is “Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet.” This exact English wording is Christopher Smart’s 1756 prose rendering (as revised by Theodore Alois Buckley in 1853) — and Horace’s own sentence doesn’t stop there: it drives on to “sapere aude, incipe” — “dare to be wise; begin!”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet; sapere aude, incipe.”
Christopher Smart (1756), rev. Theodore Alois Buckley (1853)

source.excerpt: He who postpones the hour of living well, like the hind [in the fable], waits till [all the water in] the river be run off: whereas it flows, and will flow, ever rolling on. … He has half the deed done, who has made a beginning. Boldly undertake the study of true wisdom: begin it forthwith.
trail: Horace set the line in his ‘Epistles’ (Book 1, Epistle 2, line 40, c. 20 BC); the Latin reads “Dimidium facti, qui coepit, habet; sapere aude, incipe” (Latin text ↗).
The exact English wording is Christopher Smart’s prose translation (1756), as revised by Theodore Alois Buckley (1853): “He has half the deed done, who has made a beginning” (Smart translation ↗).
Reference collections pin this precise wording to the Smart/Buckley rendering among dozens of divergent English versions of the same line (translation variants ↗).
source.excerptNote: Smart/Buckley’s prose rendering of Epistles 1.2.40–41; the bracketed gloss is the translator’s. Horace’s Latin sentence pivots from “dimidium facti…” straight into “sapere aude, incipe” — the “dare to be wise” line Kant later made a motto of the Enlightenment.

author.heading: About Horace
author.metaLine: 65 BC – 8 BC · Roman lyric poet, satirist & critic of the Augustan age
author.bio: Quintus Horatius Flaccus — “Horace” — was the leading Roman lyric poet under the emperor Augustus, celebrated for his Odes, Satires and Epistles. The Epistles are verse letters on ethics and the art of living well; Epistle 1.2 urges the young Lollius not to postpone the work of self-improvement. Horace is the source of many enduring tags, including carpe diem and sapere aude.

misattribution.heading: Genuinely Horace — but usually quoted only half-right
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Horace is sound: the thought and the Latin are his. What gets garbled is the wording and the context — the English is one translator’s choice among many, the line is habitually cut in half, and it is often blended with a different proverb.

items.why: Horace wrote Latin; “He has half the deed done, who has made a beginning” is Christopher Smart’s 1756 English, revised by Buckley in 1853. It is one of at least eighteen recorded renderings — from Drant’s 1567 “The facte begun, to one halfe is done” to Kline’s 2015 “Who’s started has half finished” (variants ↗).

items.who: Half of Horace’s line goes missing
items.why: Horace’s sentence continues “sapere aude, incipe” — “dare to be wise; begin!” The “half the deed” clause is a springboard for that exhortation, which Immanuel Kant later adopted as the motto of the Enlightenment (Wikiquote ↗).

This line is frequently conflated with the proverb “well begun is half done,” which the Oxford Dictionary of Proverbs traces first to Plato’s ‘Laws’ 753e — “the beginning is the half of every task” — and only secondarily to Horace (ODP ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The line really is Horace (Epistles 1.2.40); the familiar English is Christopher Smart’s 1756 translation, and Horace’s own sentence doesn’t end there — it presses on to “dare to be wise; begin!” (Smart translation ↗).

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Epistle 1.2 is Horace’s verse letter to the young Lollius, arguing that Homer teaches ethics better than the philosophers and that the time to start living well is now, not later. His image just before this line is of the countryman who stands at the bank waiting for the river to run dry so he can cross — “whereas it flows, and will flow, ever rolling on.” The remedy is simply to begin: “he has half the deed done who has made a beginning.”

The line’s afterlife runs through its second half. “Sapere aude” — “dare to be wise” — was lifted from this same sentence by Immanuel Kant in his 1784 essay ‘What Is Enlightenment?’ and became a rallying cry of the age of reason, which is why the “half the deed” clause is so often quoted stripped of the very words that made it famous.
